title: Design a coding judge
dek: Zotato hires engineers through a 3-hour online contest. A lakh candidates write code in the browser, press Submit, and expect a verdict in seconds: accepted, wrong answer, or too slow. Run strangers' code safely, keep it fair, and survive the rush in the last 15 minutes.

items: Submitted code is untrusted. Run it only inside a sandbox with no network, and with limits on memory, CPU time and processes, never on the servers that run your site.
Don't run code while the candidate's request waits. Save it, put its id on a queue, answer at once, and let judge workers take it from there.
The rush is known in advance: the last 15 minutes bring a quarter of all submissions. Start the extra workers before it, because new machines take minutes to boot.
A worker can die mid-run. The queue hands the job out again, and saving the verdict by submission id makes the rerun harmless.
Fairness means the same limits on the same kind of machine for everyone, with time measured as CPU time, not wall-clock time.
Candidates submit code for a problem, in one of a few languages.
Each submission is compiled and run against the problem's hidden tests; the verdict comes back in a few seconds, normally.
A live leaderboard: problems solved, then total time.
Out of scope here: the code editor itself, plagiarism checks (we'll note where they plug in), and writing the problems.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: No submission can reach the network, other submissions, or our servers
A verdict within 10 seconds, even in the last 15 minutes
The same code gets the same verdict, whenever and wherever it runs
1 lakh candidates, about 8 lakh submissions in 3 hours

items: Submissions: 8 lakh in 3 hours is about 74 a second on average.
The rush: a quarter of them, 2 lakh, arrive in the last 15 minutes. That's about 220 a second.
Work per submission: compiling plus 20 tests of about 0.1 s each is about 3 seconds of CPU.
So the rush needs about 220 × 3 = 660 cores busy at once, about 85 machines with 8 cores each. The average needs about 30.
Storage is small: 8 lakh submissions × 10 KB of code is 8 GB. Test files are a few MB per problem; every worker keeps a copy.
Problem: `id`, `title`, `statement`, `limits` (time, memory), tests in object storage.
Submission: `id`, `candidate_id`, `problem_id`, `language`, `code` (in object storage), `created_at`, `status` (queued, running, done), `verdict`, `failed_test`, `cpu_ms`.
Standing: per candidate, problems solved and total time; kept in Redis for the live leaderboard.

body.label: API
body.say: Send code and get an id back at once. Ask for its verdict, or get it pushed. Read the leaderboard a page at a time.

body.x: 202 means "accepted for judging", not "accepted as correct". The screen shows "judging…" until the verdict arrives, over a held-open connection or by asking every second or two.

body.cap: The API saves the code and puts the submission's id on a queue, then answers straight away. Judge workers take ids, run the code in a sandbox against the tests, and save the verdict. The leaderboard updates and the candidate's screen shows the result.

body.x: The API stays light: it never runs anyone's code. All the heavy, risky work happens on judge machines that hold nothing else, so a bad submission can at worst waste one sandbox's time.

body.name: First try
body.kind: RUN IT ON THE API SERVER
body.what: Write the code to a file and run it as a child process with a timeout.
body.avoid: Someone's code reads your secrets, calls the internet, fills the disk, or starts processes until the machine falls over. And it's running next to your API.
body.ex: A candidate submits a program that lists files and prints environment variables. It prints the database password.
body.like: Letting an exam candidate sit in the staff room to write their paper.

body.name: Better
body.what: Run each submission in a fresh, isolated container or small virtual machine on separate judge machines: no network, a read-only copy of the files, and hard limits on memory, CPU time, processes and output size.
body.use: A bad submission can only hurt its own sandbox, which is thrown away after the run.
body.avoid: Starting a sandbox takes time. Keep a pool of warm ones ready and reset them between runs, never reuse one dirty.
body.ex: A fork bomb hits the 64-process limit; a program printing forever hits the output limit; both get a verdict, and the machine is fine.
body.like: An exam hall: each candidate gets a clean desk, a fixed time, and nothing to take in or out.

body.cap: Inside one sandbox: no network, capped memory, CPU time and processes, read-only files. The tests run one after another; the first that fails (here test 4, over the time limit) decides the verdict, and the rest are skipped.

items: The queue absorbs the burst: candidates get their id at once, and verdicts arrive as workers free up.
But a queue only spreads the wait. At 220 a second with workers for 74, the line grows by about 150 a second, and verdicts at the end of the contest arrive minutes late, which is unfair.
The end of the contest is on the schedule, so add machines 30 minutes before it, not when the queue grows. New machines take a few minutes to boot.
Give contest submissions priority over practice runs: two queues, and workers always drain the contest one first.
Measure CPU time, not wall-clock time, so a busy neighbour on the same machine doesn't slow anyone's verdict.
Use one machine type for judging, and the same compiler versions everywhere. Publish the limits with the problem.
Penalty time comes from when the submission arrived at the API, not when a worker got to it. Waiting in the queue costs a candidate nothing.
A judge machine dies mid-run: the queue gives the job to another worker after a timeout. The verdict is saved under the submission id, so a second run only overwrites the same row.
A submission crashes the sandbox itself: it gets a "runtime error" verdict after a retry, not an endless loop of retries. Cap retries and park it for a look.
Leaderboard store lost: rebuild it from the saved verdicts. They are the record; the leaderboard is just a fast copy.
Junior / mid: a queue between submitting and judging, workers that run tests, verdicts saved and shown, a sandbox of some kind.
Senior: the sandbox limits and why, the end-of-contest numbers and scaling ahead of time, retries without double verdicts, fairness.
Lead: separate judge machines and warm sandbox pools, priority between contest and practice, rebuilding the leaderboard, where plagiarism checks plug in.
"Show partial results as tests pass?" The worker posts progress (test 7 of 20) to the submission row, and the screen reads it.
"Freeze the leaderboard in the last hour?" Keep updating the real one, but show everyone a copy taken an hour before the end. Unfreeze when the contest ends.
"Plagiarism?" After the contest, compare accepted solutions per problem in a batch job. It doesn't need to be fast.
"A new language?" A new sandbox image with its compiler and limits. Time limits may need a multiplier for slower languages.
"How do you test the judge?" Keep a set of known submissions with known verdicts, including nasty ones (fork bombs, huge output, infinite loops), and run them before every change.

body.x: The contest's last 15 minutes are a burst a queue can hold, if the workers behind it keep up. The Monday sync challenge is the same lesson.
